title: A Scots Quair
description: The great Scottish trilogy: the land, the town and the city in one woman's life, and the passage of Scotland into the modern world.
plot_or_argument: The trilogy — Sunset Song (1932), Cloud Howe (1933) and Grey Granite (1934) — follows Chris Guthrie from the Mearns croft through her marriage to a minister in the small town of Segget and her son Ewan's life as a communist agitator in the industrial city of Duncairn.
narrative_structure: Three volumes, each with its own setting and its choric openings.
principal_characters: Chris Guthrie; Ewan Tavendale; Robert Colquohoun; Ewan Colquohoun; Ellen Johns
historical_context: Scotland from 1911 to the Depression of the 1930s: the farming Mearns, the small town, and the industrial city.
literary_significance: A Scots Quair is the most complete account in fiction of Scotland's passage from the land to the city in a single generation: its three volumes, its Scots prose and its historical sweep made it the central work of the Scottish Renaissance.

title: The Story and the Fable
description: One of the finest Scottish autobiographies: Orkney, the ruined family in Glasgow, and the myth of Eden.
plot_or_argument: Muir recounts his Orkney childhood on a farm, the family's move to Glasgow and its destruction by poverty and illness, his work in a bone factory and an office, and the slow discovery of his vocation — and interprets it through the myth of the fall and the lost Eden that shapes his poetry.
narrative_structure: Autobiographical chapters interspersed with the mythic interpretation.
principal_characters: Edwin Muir; his family; Orkney; Glasgow
historical_context: The Orkney islands and the Glasgow slums of the 1890s and 1900s, the First World War, and the literary London of the 1920s.
literary_significance: The Story and the Fable is one of the great Scottish autobiographies and the key to Muir's poetry: its account of the fall from Orkney into Glasgow made the myth of Eden the centre of his work, and it is one of the finest autobiographies of the period.

title: The Narrow Place
description: Muir's finest collection: the mythic lyric of Eden, the journey and the labyrinth.
plot_or_argument: The collection contains 'The Combat', 'The Narrow Place', 'The River', 'The Return' and the poems of the journey and the dream that made Muir's reputation, in the plain mythic manner of his middle period.
narrative_structure: A collection of lyrics and short sequences.
historical_context: The Scotland of Muir's memory, the Second World War, and the mythic imagination of his middle years.
literary_significance: The Narrow Place is Muir's finest collection and the summit of the Scottish mythic lyric: its plain, unnervingly simple poems of Eden and the journey are among the finest in twentieth-century English.

title: Three Lives
description: Stein's first major work: three working-class women of Baltimore, and a prose that dismantles the nineteenth-century sentence.
plot_or_argument: The three lives — 'The Good Anna', 'Melanctha' and 'The Gentle Lena' — are those of a German servant, a Black woman and a German immigrant girl in the small town of Bridgepoint, told in a prose of repetition, present tense and simple declarative sentences that refuses the conventions of the Victorian novel.
narrative_structure: Three separate lives, each in its own section, in a prose of repetition and continuous present.
principal_characters: Anna; Melanctha Herbert; Lena; Jeff Campbell; Dr Jeff Campbell
historical_context: The Baltimore of Stein's childhood, the working-class immigrant and Black communities, and the new psychology of William James that Stein had studied at Radcliffe.
literary_significance: Three Lives is the first work of literary modernism in English by an American and the foundation of Stein's experimental prose: its repetition, its present tense and its refusal of plot made it the model for Hemingway's sentences and for a whole century of American prose.

title: Tender Buttons
description: The most radical book of the period: objects, food and rooms, in a prose that abolishes the noun's ordinary work.
plot_or_argument: The three sections — 'Objects', 'Food' and 'Rooms' — are sequences of short prose portraits of a carafe, a chair, a plate, a room, in which Stein repeats and displaces words until the object appears as a pattern of language rather than a description.
narrative_structure: Three sections of short prose pieces, arranged as a cubist still life.
historical_context: The Paris of the 1910s, the Cubist painting of Picasso and Braque that Stein was collecting, and the new avant-garde little magazines.
literary_significance: Tender Buttons is the most radical book of the period and the founding text of literary Cubism: it dissolved the descriptive sentence into pattern and repetition, and it remains the extreme limit of what prose poetry can do.

title: The Autobiography of Alice B. Toklas
description: The most entertaining memoir of the period: Stein's own life told in the voice of her companion, and the whole Paris avant-garde.
plot_or_argument: Stein writes her own autobiography in the first person of Alice B. Toklas: the San Francisco childhood, the Paris apartment at 27 rue de Fleurus, the sittings for Picasso, the Saturday evenings with Matisse, Apollinaire, Hemingway, Fitzgerald and the whole of the avant-garde, the war years and the American lecture tour.
narrative_structure: A chronological memoir in the voice of Alice B. Toklas, with an epilogue.
principal_characters: Gertrude Stein; Alice B. Toklas; Pablo Picasso; Henri Matisse; Ernest Hemingway; F. Scott Fitzgerald; Guillaume Apollinaire
literary_form: Memoir (written as if by Alice B. Toklas)
historical_context: The Paris of 1903–32, the avant-garde art world, the First World War, and the American discovery of modernism in the 1930s.
literary_significance: The Autobiography of Alice B. Toklas is the most entertaining memoir of the period and a landmark of modernist self-fashioning: it made Stein a best-seller at fifty-nine and remains the most vivid record of the Paris avant-garde.

title: Winesburg, Ohio
description: The founding book of the modern American short story: the small town as a place of hidden loneliness.
plot_or_argument: The stories follow George Willard, a young reporter on the Winesburg Eagle, through the town's inhabitants — the 'grotesques' whose lives have been twisted by an untold truth — and end with George's departure for the city.
narrative_structure: Twenty-two linked stories with an introduction and a closing departure.
principal_characters: George Willard; Wing Biddlebaum; Doctor Reefy; Elizabeth Willard; Kate Swift; Alice Hindman
historical_context: The small town of Clyde, Ohio, of Anderson's childhood, and the American small town at the moment of industrialisation.
literary_significance: Winesburg, Ohio is the founding book of the modern American short story: it made the small town a place of hidden lives, invented the linked story cycle as an American form, and its influence runs through Hemingway, Faulkner and Carver.

title: The Weary Blues
description: The first book of the Harlem Renaissance to make the blues a literary form: 'The Weary Blues', 'The Negro Speaks of Rivers'.
plot_or_argument: The collection contains 'The Weary Blues', 'The Negro Speaks of Rivers', 'Mother to Son', 'Dream Variation', 'The South' and the poems of Harlem, the cabaret and the Black South, written in the rhythms of the blues and jazz.
narrative_structure: A collection of blues poems, lyrics and songs.
historical_context: Harlem in the 1920s, the Great Migration, the blues of Bessie Smith and the cabarets of Lenox Avenue.
literary_significance: The Weary Blues put the blues on the printed page and founded the modern African American lyric: 'The Negro Speaks of Rivers' and 'The Weary Blues' are permanent poems, and the collection made Hughes the central poet of the Harlem Renaissance.

title: The Ways of White Folks
description: Hughes's finest prose: fourteen stories of the encounters between Black and white America.
plot_or_argument: The stories — 'Cora Unashamed', 'Slave on the Block', 'Home', 'The Blues I'm Playing', 'Father and Son', 'Red-Headed Baby' — dramatise the encounters of Black servants, artists, musicians and sons with the white world, in a prose of great economy and controlled anger.
narrative_structure: Fourteen stories in varied settings, from the small town to Harlem and Paris.
historical_context: The America of the early 1930s, the Harlem Renaissance's aftermath, and the encounters of race in the North and the South.
literary_significance: The Ways of White Folks is the finest prose of the Harlem Renaissance after Cane and Their Eyes Were Watching God: its fourteen stories of race made the short story a political instrument and are among the best American stories of the period.

title: Their Eyes Were Watching God
description: The finest novel of the Harlem Renaissance: Janie Crawford's three marriages, and a Black woman's voice at the centre of American fiction.
plot_or_argument: Janie Crawford, raised by her grandmother in West Florida, is married off at sixteen to an old farmer, then runs away with the ambitious Joe Starks to Eatonville, becomes the mayor's wife, and after his death falls in love with the young gambler Tea Cake. They go to the Everglades, are caught in the hurricane, and Tea Cake is bitten by a rabid dog and killed by Janie in self-defence; she returns to Eatonville alone.
narrative_structure: A framed narrative: Janie tells her story to Pheoby on her return to Eatonville.
principal_characters: Janie Crawford; Tea Cake; Joe Starks; Logan Killicks; Nanny; Pheoby Watson
historical_context: The Black towns of Florida, Eatonville, the Everglades and the migrant labour camps of the 1920s and 1930s, and the folklore that Hurston had collected as an anthropologist.
literary_significance: Their Eyes Were Watching God is the finest novel of the Harlem Renaissance and one of the great American novels of the century: its free indirect rendering of Black Southern speech, its portrait of a woman's self-making and its hurricane ending made it a permanent classic, recovered by Alice Walker in the 1970s and now central to the canon.

title: Mules and Men
description: The great record of Black Southern folklore: the lying sessions, the work songs and the Hoodoo of Florida and New Orleans.
plot_or_argument: Hurston records the folklore she collected in Eatonville, Polk County and New Orleans: the 'lying' sessions, the animal tales of Brer Rabbit and Sis Cat, the work songs, the sermons, the conjure and the Hoodoo doctors, in the voices of the men and women who told them.
narrative_structure: Two parts (Florida and New Orleans), with the folk tales transcribed in dialect.
principal_characters: Hurston herself; the storytellers of Eatonville and Polk County
historical_context: The Black rural South of the 1920s, the turpentine camps and the sawmills, and the Hoodoo tradition of New Orleans.
literary_significance: Mules and Men is the greatest record of Black Southern folklore and the founding text of African American anthropology: its transcription of the voices of the rural Black South preserved a culture that was disappearing, and it made Hurston the first Black woman to publish a book of anthropology.

title: Harlem Shadows
description: The first substantial book of verse of the Harlem Renaissance: the protest sonnet, the Jamaican dialect poem and Harlem.
plot_or_argument: The collection contains 'If We Must Die', 'The Lynching', 'America', 'The Harlem Dancer', 'Tropics in New York' and the Jamaican dialect poems — the first body of West Indian verse in English.
narrative_structure: A collection of sonnets, lyrics and dialect poems.
historical_context: Harlem in the 1920s, the Red Summer of 1919, and the Jamaica of McKay's childhood.
literary_significance: Harlem Shadows is the first substantial book of verse of the Harlem Renaissance and the collection that made the protest sonnet a modern form: 'If We Must Die' became an international anthem, and the Jamaican dialect poems founded West Indian literature in English.

title: Home to Harlem
description: The first best-selling Black novel of the decade: Jake Brown's Harlem, the cabarets and the return from the war.
plot_or_argument: Jake Brown, a Black soldier who has deserted from the army in France, returns to Harlem and lives through its cabarets, rent parties and love affairs, and goes looking for his friend Ray, a Haitian intellectual, in a novel of the Black migrant city.
narrative_structure: Three parts following Jake through Harlem, the railroad and the search for Ray.
principal_characters: Jake Brown; Ray; Felice; Zeddy; Agatha
historical_context: Harlem in the 1920s, the Great Migration, the war, and the cabaret culture of Lenox Avenue.
literary_significance: Home to Harlem was the first best-selling novel by a Black writer of the decade and the first to make Harlem's pleasure economy a literary subject: it was attacked by Du Bois for its 'licentiousness' and defended by Hughes, and the quarrel defined the Harlem Renaissance.

title: Color
description: The most formally accomplished first book of the Harlem Renaissance: 'Yet Do I Marvel', 'Heritage' and the English lyric.
plot_or_argument: The collection contains 'Yet Do I Marvel', 'Heritage', 'Incident', 'Tableau', 'From the Dark Tower' and the love lyrics that made Cullen the movement's most elegant poet.
narrative_structure: A collection of sonnets, lyrics and quatrains.
historical_context: Harlem and New York in the 1920s, the Black church and the English lyric tradition.
literary_significance: Color is the most formally accomplished first book of the Harlem Renaissance: its English lyric grace and its poems of the colour line made Cullen the movement's counterweight to Hughes, and 'Yet Do I Marvel' and 'Heritage' are permanent poems.

title: Caroling Dusk
description: The defining anthology of the Harlem Renaissance: thirty-eight Black poets, from Dunbar to the young writers of the 1920s.
plot_or_argument: Cullen's anthology gathers thirty-eight African American poets — Paul Laurence Dunbar, James Weldon Johnson, Claude McKay, Langston Hughes, Jean Toomer, Arna Bontemps, Georgia Douglas Johnson, Angelina Weld Grimké and others — with a preface defending the use of the inherited English forms.
narrative_structure: An anthology of thirty-eight poets with biographical notes.
historical_context: The Harlem Renaissance of 1925–27 and the debate over whether Black poetry should use the folk tradition or the English lyric.
literary_significance: Caroling Dusk is the defining anthology of the Harlem Renaissance and the book that fixed its canon: Cullen's preface made the case for the English tradition against Hughes's folk programme, and the anthology remains the essential collection of the movement's poetry.

title: Cane
description: The most formally radical book of the Harlem Renaissance: a collage of the Black South and the urban North.
plot_or_argument: Cane moves from the Georgia cane fields — 'Karintha', 'Fern', 'Esther', 'Blood-Burning Moon' — through the poems and prose of the migration north to Washington and Chicago, and ends with 'Kabnis', a play of a Northern Black teacher in the South.
narrative_structure: Three parts: the Georgia South, the urban North, and the play 'Kabnis'.
principal_characters: Karintha; Fern; Esther; Kabnis; Lewis; Bona; Paul
historical_context: Sparta, Georgia, where Toomer taught in 1921, and the Black migration to Washington and Chicago; the Harlem Renaissance and the new modernist art.
literary_significance: Cane is the most formally radical book of the Harlem Renaissance and one of the great American modernist texts: its collage of story, poem and drama, its lyric prose and its structure from South to North made it the only major book of the movement as formally advanced as Ulysses or The Waste Land.

title: Three Soldiers
description: One of the first great American novels of the First World War: three soldiers, the army machine and the failure of escape.
plot_or_argument: Three American soldiers — Dan Fuselli, an Italian-American from San Francisco; Chrisfield, an Indiana farm boy; and John Andrews, a Harvard-trained composer — are ground down by the army and the war; Andrews deserts to Paris and is arrested, and the novel ends with his unfinished music and his imprisonment.
narrative_structure: Three parallel lives in the army, in a naturalist narrative.
historical_context: The American army in the First World War, the camps and the front, the military machine that destroys its soldiers, and the post-war disillusion of the American intellectual.
literary_significance: Three Soldiers was one of the first great American novels of the First World War and the founding work of the American anti-war novel: its naturalism and its anger changed the American treatment of the war, and it made Dos Passos the most promising young novelist of his generation.

title: Manhattan Transfer
description: The first great American novel of the modern city: New York in the 1920s, in a montage of lives, newsreels and songs.
plot_or_argument: The novel follows a large cast through New York in the first decades of the century — Ellen Thatcher, Jimmy Herf, George Baldwin, Congo Jake — in a montage of narrative, newspaper headlines and song lyrics, moving from the immigrant arrival to the boom of the 1920s.
narrative_structure: A montage of many lives in five parts, interspersed with newspaper headlines and songs.
principal_characters: Ellen Thatcher; Jimmy Herf; George Baldwin; Congo Jake; Anna Cohen
historical_context: New York in the 1900s–20s, the immigrant city, the boom and the new mass culture of the movies, the tabloids and the advertising.
literary_significance: Manhattan Transfer is the first great American novel of the modern city and the direct forerunner of U.S.A.: its montage of lives, headlines and songs invented the American collective novel.

title: U.S.A.
description: The most ambitious American novel of the period: the history of America from 1900 to 1930 through twelve lives, newsreels and biographies.
plot_or_argument: The trilogy — The 42nd Parallel (1930), Nineteen Nineteen (1932) and The Big Money (1936) — follows twelve Americans from the 1900s to the Wall Street crash, interrupted by the Newsreel (headlines and songs), the Camera Eye (the author's autobiographical prose poems) and the biographies of public figures from Eugene Debs to Woodrow Wilson.
narrative_structure: Three volumes, each in four strands (narrative, Newsreel, Camera Eye, biography).
principal_characters: Mac; J. Ward Moorehouse; Janey Williams; Eleanor Stoddard; Charley Anderson; Mary French; Ben Compton
historical_context: America from 1900 to 1930: the labour movement, the First World War, the Red Scare, Prohibition, the boom and the crash.
literary_significance: U.S.A. is the most ambitious American novel of the period and the founding work of the collective documentary novel: its four-strand technique invented a form for writing the history of a nation in fiction.

title: The Great Gatsby
description: The most nearly perfect American novel: Jay Gatsby's dream, Daisy Buchanan and the green light at the end of the dock.
plot_or_argument: Nick Carraway, a young bond salesman from the Midwest, rents a house on Long Island next to the mysterious Jay Gatsby, who gives lavish parties in the hope of attracting Daisy Buchanan, the married woman he loved before the war. The affair, the confrontation in the Plaza Hotel and the death of Myrtle Wilson end in Gatsby's murder and Nick's disillusioned return west.
narrative_structure: Nine chapters narrated by Nick Carraway, in a retrospective and tightly patterned structure.
principal_characters: Jay Gatsby; Nick Carraway; Daisy Buchanan; Tom Buchanan; Jordan Baker; Myrtle Wilson; George Wilson
historical_context: Long Island and New York in the summer of 1922, the jazz age, Prohibition, the old money of the Buchanans and the new money of the bootlegger.
literary_significance: The Great Gatsby is the most nearly perfect American novel and the definitive book of the 1920s: its lyric prose, its structure and its meditation on the American dream made it the great American novel of the century, and its last page is among the most famous in American literature.
